reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: An indolent mature B-cell malignancy classically presenting with pancytopenia, monocytopenia and marked splenomegaly, often without lymphadenopathy
The blood film shows characteristic lymphoid cells with fine cytoplasmic hairy projections
Monocytopenia is a useful and fairly specific clue that helps distinguish it from other lymphoproliferative disorders
The immunophenotype is a clonal B cell expressing CD11c, CD25, CD103 and CD123, and annexin-A1 positivity is highly characteristic
The BRAF V600E mutation is present in nearly all classic cases and is the defining molecular lesion
Marrow aspiration is frequently a dry tap because of reticulin fibrosis, so a trephine biopsy showing a fried-egg appearance is important
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) positivity is a traditional cytochemical hallmark, and treatment centres on purine analogues, with BRAF inhibition for relapsed or refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Hairy cell leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes with distinctive cytoplasmic projections. The near-universal driver is the activating BRAF V600E mutation, which switches on the RAF-MEK-ERK signalling pathway and promotes survival and characteristic morphology and adhesion properties. The malignant cells infiltrate the bone marrow, inducing reticulin fibrosis that explains the frequent dry tap, and populate the splenic red pulp producing splenomegaly. Marrow infiltration and hypersplenism together drive the pancytopenia and the characteristic monocytopenia that increases infection risk.
additionalDifferentials: Hairy cell leukaemia variant (now a distinct entity)
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film to identify hairy cells and monocytopenia
Flow cytometry (CD11c, CD25, CD103, CD123) and annexin-A1 staining
Bone marrow trephine biopsy with reticulin stain
Molecular testing for BRAF V600E mutation
redFlags: Severe neutropenia or monocytopenia with serious or opportunistic infection
Symptomatic massive splenomegaly or splenic rupture
Failure to respond to purine analogue therapy suggesting the variant form
Progressive marrow failure with bleeding or transfusion dependence
reference.prognosis: Classic hairy cell leukaemia responds well to purine analogue therapy with durable remissions and near-normal life expectancy for many patients; relapses can occur but often respond to further treatment or BRAF-targeted therapy.
pitfalls: Interpreting a dry marrow tap as inadequate rather than a diagnostic clue for fibrosis
Confusing it with splenic marginal zone lymphoma or the hairy cell variant, which behave differently
Overlooking monocytopenia as a diagnostic pointer
Missing BRAF V600E testing that confirms classic disease and guides targeted therapy
management: Purine nucleoside analogue therapy with cladribine or pentostatin as the first-line mainstay, achieving durable remissions
Rituximab combined with, or following, a purine analogue to deepen response and eradicate minimal residual disease
BRAF inhibitor therapy such as vemurafenib for relapsed or refractory disease harbouring the BRAF V600E mutation
Defer treatment until cytopenias or symptomatic splenomegaly develop, observing asymptomatic patients
Antimicrobial prophylaxis and vigilance for opportunistic infection because of the characteristic monocytopenia, with red cell and platelet transfusion support
Consider splenectomy for massive or refractory symptomatic splenomegaly in selected patients
Regular full blood count and clinical surveillance to detect and re-treat relapse
